speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF FILING DATE FOR 1942 RETURNS
speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue. May I ask whether the time can be extended beyond June 30 for the filing of income tax returns for 1942, more particularly under T-l general? It is pointed out to me by chartered accountants and business firms that in many cases it will be impossible for them to file their returns by that date and they contend that they should not be subjected to penalties or excessive interest charges. There have been changes in tax legislation and delays in the printing of the legislation and forms, which have been only recently distributed. Moreover, the staffs of chartered accountants and the offices of business concerns have been depleted by enlistments and by the transference of men to government work, and these have been replaced by inexperienced help. In addition to that, the work has greatly increased and many of these firms of chartered accountants find it impossible to make up their returns as of June 30.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. W. G. GIBSON (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF FILING DATE FOR 1942 RETURNS
speechtext:
The hon. member was good enough to give me notice of his question. Income tax returns which are due on June 30 are the individual returns, and the returns of corporations whose years ended on December 31. While amendments to the act delayed the production of the 1942 income tax forms,
taxpayers have had six months in which to determine their 1942 incomes, and the forms have been available since early this month. There still remain over two weeks in which to file these returns.
I realize that some congestion exists in the offices of chartered accountants, who have numerous returns to prepare, but in view of the large number of taxpayers who will be filing returns, and the millions of dollars payable this month, it is not considered advisable to postpone the collection of this large sum by a general extension of time.

speakeroldname: Mr. LIONEL CHEVRIER (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to discuss briefly this afternoon a subject which I believe is of some importance in the consideration of the war appropriation resolution so far as it concerns the Department of Munitions and Supply; that is, the purchasing policy of the department. For a moment I want to consider the method adopted in the department to reduce costs and to control profit margins. I should like to discuss briefly the contracting policy of the department, the manner in which contracts are awarded, the various kinds of contracts, the controls exercised over them, some of the conservation methods that have been adopted by the direc-tors-general and the consequent reduction in prices of many of the commodities and instruments of war purchased by the department. These are all matters which have been discussed in the house from time to time, and I should like to show that the job of the department is to get the maximum possible value for the taxpayer's dollar, which involves not only seeing that profits are fair and reasonable bu't that costs are driven down in every possible way.
The chief job of the Department of Munitions and Supply is that of procurement for the army, the navy and the air force of Canada, the United Kingdom and the united nations. Its first job is to procure as quickly as possible those things which may be required from time to time. In the first years of the war the department was criticized because it was not producing fast enough. Now that production is here the main criticism seems to be that we are producing too fast and that the programme is costing far too much. I should like to examine that charge in the light of methods adopted by the department and the procedure followed to reduce costs and curtail profit margins. Before going into that subject, however, there are three points which I believe deserve the attention of the committee. The first point is that Canada, has never
TMr. Speaker.]
been a manufacturer of military, naval or aircraft stores. We had not made a single gun in this country prior to the war. Certainly we had never made a tank, and for somt twenty-five years prior to the war I do not believe we had produced a merchant shipping vessel. It is true that we had made son*' commercial planes but we had never made a combat plane, and I am sure hon. members will agree that there is all the difference in the world between a commercial and a combat plane.

We had
built commercial shipping.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
My suggestion was that within a period of twenty-five years prior to the war we had not produced cargo or merchant shipping vessels. I was going on to say that the department was faced with this position, that it had to purchase a huge quantity of military stores never before made in this country. It would go to a manufacturer and ask him to make these articles. The manufacturer, not having made them before, was faced with the difficulty of not being able to submit a price. Very often he would say to the officers of the department, "Do you know what it is going to cost?" The answer from us was no, because we had no further information than he had in regard to costs. Therefore it became necessary to negotiate on the subject of prices, and the difficulty resulted from the fact that the contractor not only had not made these implements of war previously but did not know the price to quote, any more than the department knew it.
The second point I wish to bring to the attention of the committee is that all those who have given this subject any thought have come to the conclusion that the most desirable kind of contract that could be negotiated, under those circumstances was the fixed, price contract, in which the contractor undertakes to furnish to the department a fixed number of articles at so many cents or so many dollars. That is the ordinary contract that everyone was accustomed to in peace time. Obviously it has many advantages, because the contractor takes all the risks. Then the third/ point arose, but how are you going to negotiate safely fixed price contracts upon stores that not only have never been made in this country before but concerning the prices of which neither the department nor the contractor had the slightest idea?
That was the fundamental problem of munitions and supply in connection with the purchasing of a great deal of the military stores that it required from time to time. The department therefore had to establish a policy

War Appropriation-Supplies
and set up a technique. Briefly summed up, this is what was evolved. Wherever possible the competitive price system is used as the best method of finding the most efficient contractor. The department thinks that the cheapest production, both from the point of view of cost as well as the point of view of profits, can be obtained through the negotiation of short term contracts on a fixed price basis. However, the success of contracts of this kind depends entirely upon the ability of the department to obtain full, accurate and up to date knowledge of the costs of the contractor. Where this is not possible and cannot be obtained, as in the case of tanks and certain guns which have as many as 2,400 parts, the department has had to work out variations and modifications of the fixed price contract.
Here let me note that four-sevenths, in point of number, of all the contracts awarded by the Department of Munitions and Supply have been on the fixed price basis.
Though some criticize the tender system, the department adheres to the view that if we can get real competition between two or more concerns we are likely to get low prices on the first order and still lower prices on subsequent orders. Practically all purchases of foodstuffs, barracks stores, supplies, clothing and equipment of that kind have been purchased on the tender system. Obviously, however, the tender system will not work out when applied to the purchase of equipment mostly technical in character, which has never been produced in this country before. The department therefore hit upon the expedient of the cost audit. It allowed the manufacturer a reasonable fee for his work, with the understanding that at the earliest possible date it would examine his costs and revise his price as his costs might warrant.
Contracts, as a general rule, and in a broad way, which are awarded in the department may be divided into two parts, those awarded to independent contractors and those negotiated by so-called agents. The independent contracts may in turn be subdivided into five parts the first of which is the fixed price contract, about which I have been speaking; the next is the ceiling price contract, about which I shall have something to say in a moment. It is the contract which has to do generally speaking with the purchase of mechanical transport. Then there is the unit fee contract used generally in the purchase of guns. Again, we have another division called the target price; and finally the cost plus percentage. This is of course the least desirable kind of contract. But there are some instances when resort must be had to it, as for instance the case of overhaul of
aircraft, and repair contracts for aircraft. But it is only in exceptional circumstances that resort is had to that kind of contract.
Contracts entered into by so-called agents may also be subdivided into two parts, those negotiated by government-owned companies, and those negotiated by privately owned companies on a management fee basis. Government-owned companies may be either operating companies, such as Small Arms Limited, or supervising companies, such as Allied War Supplies Limited. And the management fee contract may be on a unit basis, a monthly basis or a yearly basis.
These are the general divisions of contracts in the department. There are other contracts of an exceptional nature to which I make no reference here. Where the contractor is able to give us a fixed price, which we have reason to believe is fairly close to the right price we negotiate with him what is called a ceiling price contract. This means that the contractor's costs will be audited when the job is done, and he will be paid the actual audited costs, plus a fee, or a percentage on costs. In no case will the cost plus profit exceed the ceiling agreed upon. If on audit it is found that the ceiling price exceeds the actual cost plus the agreed profit, the contractor must adjust his price and return the excess he has been paid. This is what is called the ceiling price contract. It is subject to revision downward only.
Another type of arrangement in lieu of fixed price negotiations had to be found in the case where a reputable manufacturer was unable to submit any reasonable estimate of his costs, and was willing to work for a settled period without any fixed price. In such case it was our policy to allow the contractor his actual audited costs, plus a fee of so many dollars or cents for each unit of output which passed inspection. Sometimes the changing character of the contract necessitated a percentage rather than a fee. However, as I said a moment ago we have used the percentage on cost arrangement only as a last resort, and where it was quite impossible to estimate the duration or the difficulties of the job.
A word about the unit fee. This arrangement has a definite bearing on speed of production. The sooner the manufacturer gets his first unit out, the sooner he begins to earn something for his operation. The more units he produces, the higher are his earnings. The unit fee method has had much to do with the speeding up of production and the reduction of costs.
The question is sometimes asked: How can the cost plus fee arrangement lead to low
War Appropriation-Supplies

costs? Where is the incentive? The answer is that you do not speed production without a more efficient use of mam-power. And where you reduce the number of man-hours required for a certain job, you also reduce its costs. So that the incentive to speed also creates an incentive to cost reduction.
At the start of a programme the manufacturer usually gets a large number of employees around him, in order to speed up production. Gradually he will find this to be somewhat cumbersome, and will always reduce the number of his employees later on, as the programme advances, in order to obtain more efficiency. This inevitably will lead to lower costs.
Still another method for creating incentive for cost reduction, where a fixed price cannot be established at the beginning of a programme, is the target price contract. The target price is something for the contractor to shoot at. It is really a trial run on the preliminary part of the programme. If the contractor gets under the target he will get a profit. If he goes over the target he will be penalized. Under this plan the contractor agrees to accept the target price for the first five or ten per cent of the amount of his contract. If after an audit it is found that the actual cost is the same as the target, the contractor gets a profit of five per cent of the target. If the contractor's costs exceed the target his profit is reduced by twenty-five per cent of the excess over and above the target. Should his actual costs be less than the target, he gets a bonus of twenty-five per cent of the saving. On this type of contract frequent audits are made sometimes as often as every three months.
So that we finally arrive at the position where it is possible to negotiate with the contractor a fixed price contract. I should like to point out, Mr. Chairman, that all these various modifications of the fixed price contract, such as the target price, the ceiling price and the unit fee arrangement are temporary arrangements being used by the department pending the day when it will be possible to negotiate contracts on a fixed price basis.
One of the great difficulties about establishing fixed prices is the frequent change in the design of equipment while it is in production. There is no known way of determining the efficiency of war equipment, except by use in combat. We find we must ask our contractors to make frequent changes in the design of equipment. Had it not been for these modifications and variations of the fixed price contract, production would certainly never have attained the peak it has attained 
to-day. The best proof of the wisdom of our policy is that to-day there exists in the department a group of war contractors who are definitely cost conscious. Their interest in cost reduction is second only to their interest in production.
I should like now to pass on to the checks or controls which are exercised in the department over contracts of a cost-plus nature. These are three in number: First, the treasury cost accountant; second, the representatives of Munitions and Supply, and third, the directors-general of the various programmes.
The cost accountant is an official of the Department of Finance. He is attached to the treasury branch of that department, and he works hand in hand with the Department of Munitions and Supply. There are hundreds of these cost accountants scattered throughout war industries in the country. Their job is to find out what costs are, and to supervise those costs. These men operate in accordance with a strict formula. For the information of the committee I should like to table the costing memorandum of the Department of Munitions and Supply, known as No. 433. This memorandum sets out in detail the items which may be charged as items of cost and those which may not be. I can assure you that there is no provision for donations, entertainment expenses, advertising expenses, bank interest and the like. If hon. members are interested in this costing memorandum and will read it, they will find there in great detail all the items which may or which may not be charged as cost items.
The cost accountant does not confine himself in his investigation to what the books show. He inquires into matters such as scrap losses, quantities and costs of materials, use of man-hours and things of that kind which are not normally shown on a company's books. He tries by a spot investigation to make sure that the company's payroll is genuine and has not been padded. He tries to bring into relief all substantial or unreasonable salary increases or bonuses which may not appear on the surface. He segregates and isolates expenses incidental to the development of a programme and which are not likely to recur in its advanced stages. He aims to tell the department the story of what is going on in the industry with reference to cost; he tries to tell the department not only the cost during the first period of production but also the cost after production is well under way. Where such costs are obtained the department is then in position to negotiate fixed price contracts.

War Appropriation-Supplies
The representatives of Munitions and Supply are experienced officials of the department -who operate in the large war industries, particularly those on a cost plus fee basis. It is the responsibility of these men to help the industry increase production and reduce costs. They are also required to report all cases of inefficient or uneconomical operation. The directors-general of production supervise and direct all programmes. With their associates and assistants they combine the best production and technical experience that is available in the country.
For some time past the production departments under the direction of the coordinator of production have begun a campaign of conservation, the object of which is to help the contractors conserve machine tools, manhours and materials of a critical nature. When this campaign was exhibited in Toronto in October last year it was estimated that at that time it had saved the country some $155,000,000. The estimate to-day would unquestionably be much higher. This exhibit of conservation projects was afterwards moved from Toronto and may now be seen in Montreal. If there are some hon. members who have not seen this exhibit I would suggest to them that they could profitably spend the time necessary to go to see it. It is now at 1155 Bishop street, Montreal. I am informed by one of the directors of this branch that some time next week the exhibit will be moved to Ottawa, where it may be seen.
I should like to give to the committee four or five examples taken from this conservation project which I believe will speak volumes for what has been done in the campaign, (a) First, I should like to refer to what has been accomplished in -connection with the body of the Bren gun. This body is made from a steel forging, and after certain experiments it was found possible to redesign the forging dies so that it would be nearer to the finished Shape. This resulted in a saving of 1,200,000 pounds of stainless steel and a large amount of chrome, which is scarce. Owing to the improved shape, 10,000 man-hours have been saved in the machining of this one part. A value of $125,000 may safely be put upon the saving in connection with this one item.
(b) The small catch for the Bren gun magazine was originally built up with welding rod and then machined to shape. It was found possible to accomplish the same purpose by three press operations, and the result has been a saving of 198,000 pounds of welding rod, and $39,000 worth of oxygen and acetylene. The saving in labour has been 515,000 hours and ten
machine tools have been eliminated. The value of this conservation project is about $329,000. (c) The bipod assembly on the Boys anti-tank rifle was redesigned to be made from a malleable iron casting instead of from a steel forging, steel tubing and bar stock. The annual saving here has been estimated at 771,600 pounds of steel forgings, and forging capacity is very tight; 72,000 pounds of seamless steel tubing, which is scarce and has to be imported; 164,500 pounds of bar steel; 477,600 hours of labour and 77 machine tools. We can value this project at $1,780,000.
(d) The fuse for the 25-pounder shell was originally machined from brass bar stock. Brass calls for copper, which is extremely critical. The fuse was re-engineered to be made from zinc die castings. This resulted in saving 44,000,000 pounds of brass. At the same'time 816,000 hours of labour were saved annually and fifteen machine tools were eliminated from this operation. This conservation project can be valued at over $6,500,000. (e) I should like to select one example from several hundred successful changes which have been made in the universal carrier. The track sprocket was originally rough flame cut from steel plate and partly finish machined all over. Now the sprocket is made from centrifugally cast steel and the only machining necessary is the boring of the. hole for the shaft and the drilling of a few small holes. The annual saving in plate stock is nearly 9,000,000 pounds; 725,000 hours of labour have been saved, and the total saving can be valued at $1,700,000.
(/) Not all the ingenuity of this campaign has been directed toward war stores. Here is a case concerning the packing of motor vehicles for overseas shipment. A change was made in the manufacturing of the truck, which made closer packing possible. A study of the building of the boxes as to use of lumber and nails was made. This resulted in a large saving of shipping space, as well as a saving of 3,635 freight cars, over $2,000,000 worth of nails and lumber, and over $1,000,000 in labour. I would point out that no one can put a value on the shipping space which was saved.
The technical and financial press has been awake to the significance of this great conservation movement which is rapidly assuming the aspect of a crusade and it has spread the news of the accomplishments throughout Canadian industry. All these examples of savings were selected from a group of over 500 reported to the department some months ago. To them must be added over 350 more itemp reported in recent months.
All this information naturally raises the question of what has happened to prices in relation thereto. In addition to the greater

I am advised by the munitions contracts branch that the quarterly review of fixed prices on ammunition components for the second quarter of 1943, as compared with the first quarter, indicates a total over-all saving of $2^ million.
Gratifying as these results are, they do not permit of any complacency. Critical shortages still face us. The. need for the most frugal use of man-power still exists.
One most encouraging feature of to-day's picture is the earnest participation of the workers themselves in making their labour more fruitful. "Employee suggestion plans'' are being installed in plants throughout Canada. Canadian workers, stimulated by fair systems of recognition and rewards, have turned in thousands of usable ideas. Many are small in importance by themselves, but when multiplied by the thousand, they assume gigantic proportions. It is too early to try to make any estimate of the total savings which will be made by Canadian workmen, but here is a sample from one industry only which will indicate the possibilities. In this one industry during the period from August 22, 1942, to April 3, 1943, no fewer than 4,512 suggestions were received from the workers, of which 460 have been accepted and put into production, and over 1,200 have yet to be studied. In that industry the workers have been awarded $21,352.65 for their suggestions.

I would like to say a word now, if I may about renegotiation. Notwithstanding the precautions taken by the department to reduce costs and curtail profit margins, occasionally there develops a case where the profit on a fixed price contract is an inordinate one. This may develop where large volumes of material or equipment of a certain kind have to be obtained. When this occurs the department takes the view that the contractor in *war time should be content to give the taxpayer the greater part of the benefit of the improved techniques, rather than retain them for himself.
While the department appreciates the principle of the sanctity of contracts entered into between itself and its contractors, still it realizes that in war time there is a responsibility placed upon the minister to protect the taxpayers' money. For this reason, where it is shown that profits are unreasonable, the department renegotiates contracts, first, voluntarily, and then on a compulsory basis if need be. The powers in this regard conferred upon the minister, are to be found in clause 13, subsection 4, of the bill which was passed by the house some weeks ago. The subsection reads as follows:
Renegotiate contract price.
(4) If the minister is satisfied, upon an examination of the accounts and records of a person who has entered into a munitions contract, that the contract price paid and payable to such person contains an unreasonable profit, he may direct such person to renegotiate the contract price and may direct that there be withheld from such person any amount of the contract price which in the opinion of the minister represents an unreasonable profit, and may direct such person to pay to the Receiver General of Canada forthwith any amount which such person has received which in the opinion of the minister represents an unreasonable profit.
Then again, there is the control exercised over war profits by the corporation income tax and the excess profit tax. Following the budget of the year 1942, a company would1 pay at least 40 per cent of total profits as a corporation tax and an excess profit tax of 10 per cent of the net income, or 100 per cent of the excess profit over the average for the standard period. No change has been made with reference to these taxes in the budget which was brought down this year. Under existing tax laws no corporation can earn, after tax, a greater amount that seventy per cent of its pre-war standard profit.
It will be seen therefore, Mr. Chairman, from what I have been saying that the job of munitions supply may be subdivided into three parts, which in order of importance are: (1) to secure the required output in the minimum of

War Appropriation-Supplies
time; (2) to secure all benefits of modern production and cost reduction technique; and (3) to keep profits under strict control.
* I do not pretend, Mr. Chairman, that we have attained one hundred per cent efficiency in all these, but all in all we are doing a good job in spending the taxpayers' money.
Mr. HA'NSON (York Sunbury): You are spending enough money all right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
There is no doubt of that, but my contention is that we are doing a good job in spending that money and we are trying to negotiate contracts on a proper, sound and businesslike basis. We are maintaining a close check on costs and profits through the audit system, and we are seeking to improve manufacturing technique by daily contact between our production officials and our contractors.
I should like to quote here what some people who do not live in this country think of our system, and I say this, that notwithstanding the criticism which may from time to time have been levelled against the control of war profits in Canada our system is more efficient than that at the present time obtaining in the United States. I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the "University of Pennsylvania Law Review/' It is from the pen of James R. Withrow, Jr. Mr. Withrow is a graduate of Cornell university and a member of the New York Bar. He wrote an article entitled "The Control of War Profits in the United States and Canada." He came to Canada and spent some time here studying the methods which we adopted, in order to compare them with those exercised in the United States. In this rather lengthy article he goes into the manner in which the country to the south handles costs and profit margins as compared with the manner which we adopted, and he concludes in this fashion: I quote two sentences from his concluding paragraphs:
Canada's method of controlling war profits is to negotiate contracts carefully and for a short period of time, and to provide wherever possible, an incentive to the manufacturer to reduce his costs. The tax laws are left to take care of the rest. . . .
And the concluding sentence:
Certainly Canada's policy of awarding war contracts for short terms and subject to continuous scientific cost inspection, and thereafter relying on high corporate and excess profits taxes, seems better adapted to eliminate war profits without any discouragement of production than the procedures which have been followed in the United States.
Canadians might well be proud of the fact that, after almost four years of war, with an unprecedented outlay of public funds,
there have been few charges of graft and almost no accusations of improper use of war moneys. In the few cases where waste and dishonesty have been discovered, the department has acted quickly and effectively.
The department is most anxious to maintain its reputation for honesty and efficiency. That it has done so in the face of many obstacles is due not only to the checks and controls which I have been speaking of, but particularly to the high calibre of the men who administer the war programme.

I rise to take part in this phase of the committee's discussions in order to deal with two points only, and those at not very great length.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply, in his statement to the house the other day, pictured the development of a department which, judging by the buildings it occupies in Ottawa alone, seems to be almost an empire in itself. I take it that his statement was intended as a tribute to the energy, the capacity and the determination of Canadians in industry and in labour circles so far as the prosecution of our war effort to a successful issue is concerned. Sometimes we tend to divide ourselves into sections in our attitude to the war effort. That is a mistake. All Canada-every one of us-is in this effort; and, assuming the minister desired to express his commendation of those who are engaged in the production of materials of war, I would endorse that expression. I would, however, point out that since the administrative end of the department has developed into this huge empire, perhaps some criticism of a constructive nature may properly be directed to the minister in charge and to the government.
So far as industrial production goes, the government has adopted the policy of employer and employee production committees sometimes known as labour-management production committees. Their objective, of course, is increased production. The government, being committed to the encouragement of employer and employee production committees throughout the industries of the nation, must accept some criticism in view of the fact that it has not set an example by applying this principle in the administrative branch of the Department of Munitions and Supply. I mentioned this in a previous discussion without enlarging on it. Members of parliament have had placed in their hands a chart displaying the structure of the minister's department. Most of us who are interested in labour are concerned to find that, in the whole of this giant administrative

War Appropriation-Supplies
organization, the closest if not the only approach to labour cooperation is represented by the appointment held by Doctor Goldenberg, the liaison officer with the Department of Labour.
I am in hearty agreement with the policy and purpose of employer-employee production committees. We have too long ignored the fact that if we are to go places in production in any line, we must have a partnership of industry and labour. One of the best places where the government could realize, this objective is right in the top strata of the Department of Munitions and Supply itself.
I would pay my tribute at this time to the industrialists who have given of their time and energies and abilities to the work over which the minister has jurisdiction. My criticism in no way constitutes a reflection on anyone, whether he be in labour or industry, who is giving of his best. It stems from the fact that in this departmental empire, labour has not its proper place and is not enabled to take its proper part. Hon. members know that in Great Britain organized labour has become a major partner in the national effort. We all admire the attitude of British labour and its accomplishments during the war. To use a phrase frequently employed by the Minister of Labour when the history of the war-time endeavour of Great Britain is written, the contribution of British labour will stand out in bold relief.
I would therefore urge upon the minister, with all the earnestness at my command, and believing that we who have been champions of labour in this house and outside it for *many years may properly make this suggestion, that he take labour into fuller partnership in the work of his department. The complaint is made not only with respect to the Department of Munitions but with respect to other departments of government as well, that agriculture and labour, embracing as they do two great producing elements of our country, have not, during this period of war, been taken sufficiently into the partnership so as to ensure the most vigorous and effective prosecution of the war.
I come to another point. Now that we have read so much and heard so much about making the world safe for democracy, to most of us who have not during the past been associated with major business enterprises, but have been ordinary common people trying to get along, making the world safe for democracy means at the same time making it safe for the common man. That is one of the things which we are prone to forget; because if the world is to remain safe for democracy it must

be a world in which the little man has his place and his proper share of the opportunities of life. I lay that down as the premise of what I am about to say.
I have always felt that those who represent the bigger interests in this country and in other countries as well are able to speak for themselves. It can properly be said that they have not been exactly inarticulate in the years that are past. But it is the duty of those who represent the people in this parliament, as it is the duty of those who represent the people in other legislative assemblies throughout the world, to raise our voices on behalf of the little man; because very often his voice cannot otherwise be heard.
Yesterday we saw an amazing performance, at least so far as I was concerned. Looking on it as one who was attempting to gauge the position of those who were contending one way or the other, I could not help thinking that in the statement given by the Minister of Munitions and Supply there was a certain helplessness with regard to his position and that of the government. I am not going to attach a lot of blame to the Minister of Munitions and Supply particularly. I simply wish to attack a system which leaves him in a position of helplessness such as his words themselves would indicate on an occasion of this kind. Surely in Canada we have not yet reached the stage where a government need suffer from creeping paralysis in relation to international combinations with which it has sometimes to come in contact and with which it has to deal.
It is true, with respect to the contract as to which there was so much discussion yesterday and last night, that there are four nations involved, namely, Great Britain, the United States, Australia and Canada. It may be argued one way and then another with regard to the price which was paid for the product of these plants. But whatever may have been the underlying factor in the matter of price, I think it must have been made abundantly clear that at least the company involved was not losing anything in the transaction. Moreover, it seemed to me that the minister himself was not too sure that the actual price itself was the price that he would have placed upon the product. Rather, he left the impression that the price was set and that the governments of these four nations acquiesced and bought the product at a figure, not that they had thought was the proper one, but one that was set by an international combination.
Perhaps the government may be able to argue that from the point of view of selfish

War Appropriation-Supplies
nationalism Canada might conceivably get a better deal out of the transaction than the other three. That is not a sufficient answer. It is not a sufficient answer to say that the Minister of Finance will be able to hold his pail and get some of the milk out of the whole arrangement by way of taxation. There is a broader and much more comprehensive picture.
Millions of working people in Canada, and the men and women on 750,000 farms, are trying to find for themselves a field for private initative and private enterprise and for free enterprise itself. When the minister speaks as he did about his first job being to fight this war, no one will disagree on that point. But when he speaks of fighting the war and not fighting international combines, it seems to me that this might perhaps be a proper statement to make if the minister at the beginning had been able to assure the committee that while the war was being fought the same international combines were not fighting a battle against the common people themselves. Then it becomes a question not of attack but of defence, and I wish to draw that to the minister's attention, because while we are fighting this war we must be careful that there are no interests, international or otherwise, that are attacking either economically or financially the common people, whether they be working men, farmers, or members of other sections of the community.
Of course mention was made of other interests than that which occupied most of the attention of the committee yesterday. I shall not deal with them except to say that it does indicate, I think, a condition of affairs bo which the declaration of the Progressive Conservative party, which met in Winnipeg last December, is pertinent. The party at that convention found it desirable and1 necessary, in the national interest, to make this public declaration which I wish to put on the record:
Every person able and willing to work must be assured of gainful occupation with sufficient means to maintain a home and family. The objective is full employment at fair wages under progressively improving standards. We oppose relief as a substitute for work. For the achievement of this objective-
And now I come to the point which I wish particularly to emphasize.
For the achievement of that objective-full employment at fair wages under progressively improving standards

and for the welfare and development of society, we strongly advocate the strengthening of the basic Canadian tradition of individual initiative and individual enterprise and opportunity, and the freeing of economic activities from bureaucratic controls. Government authority, however, should be maintained and exercised wherever necessary to. protect
primary producers, workers and consumers from exploitation through such abuses as price-fixing combines, monopolies and patent cartels. To those ends we believe that government should seek to create conditions under which the maximum volume of employment and the maximum national income may be assured through the initiative and enterprise of the people themselves.
Having in mind the desires of those who wish to follow the doctrine of individual initiative and free enterprise, which is in the interests of the people generally, in my opinion international combinations and cartels constitute one of the principal impediments to the achievement of this objective by the little man, whether he be in business, on the farm, in other primary occupations, in the workshop, in the plant or in the factory. Therefore these combinations, it seems to m,e, may well be the enemy of the ordinary man, and for that reason I raise my voice this afternoon in respect to this matter.
More than that; while it may be said that our friends to the left are very voluble in their criticism of this particular company, I suggest that while it is always necessary to arouse public opinion in regard to matters which need correction, it is equally important, if not more so, that the solution should be brought forward at the same time that the difficulty is outlined. I do not say this in any small, critical way of the group which brought up this matter yesterday, but I do believe that free enterprise and individual initiative never can find their true place in a world order in which monopolistic combinations exist; nor do I think that place can be found in a world order in which socialism is rampant. So as far as this party is concerned, our desire is expressed in the words which I read from the policy embodied in the convention platform, and I think that is one thing upon which the people of Canada will be generally agreed.
I should like to say a word in reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier), who is the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply and who spoke this afternoon. The hon. member made it abundantly clear that as far as his department is concerned the problem of the renegotiation or adjustment of contracts could be dealt with on a voluntary basis; but he took care to indicate that the department would not hesitate to deal with these matters by compulsory methods in connection with contracts which they considered to be unfair, and he pointed out that the act gave the department power to proceed in this way. Following that statement I have a suggestion to offer in regard to the contract which has been under discussion. In the first place it seems
War Approbation-Supplies

to me, as I think it must seem to the government and the minister, that this is a contract which in the interests of the Canadian people as well as the interests of the united nations should be reviewed and renegotiated. There is no reason in the world why Canada should not take the lead with respect to the whole question of international combinations. I do not think this country wants to take a back seat, in comparison with other countries in the world, in exercising initiative with respect to the formation of a new order when this war is over. I like to think that this nation will be in the front line when it comes to worldwide reform, as we want to see this country in the front with respect to domestic reform.
Having that definitely in mind, together with the information that is available in respect to international combinations throughout the world, it seems to me that this country should at once take the lead in setting up an international body which would go into the whole question of these combinations; because, from the minister's own statement, this country would seem helpless to do it alone. Perhaps some will say we should have a royal commission to look into the allegations that have been made with respect to this company, and I would be in favour of that; I put myself on record in that respect now. But I think more than a royal commission in Canada is required; I think we need a commission having power to cover the whole gamut of the united nations. Since this war began we have gone a long way in bringing together representatives of the various nations to discuss different subjects. We have had a conference on the question of food, for instance, and there are other matters which are the prospective subjects of further conferences of the kind. But if we are to clear away the underbrush which may bar the pathway to peace in the years following this war we must undertake some of the hard things as well as some of the easier things, and I think Canada ought now to take the initiative in the formation of an international body which will see to it that in the years to come, whether we are at peace or at war, no group of people other than governments will be able to exercise almost super-governmental powers. I believe the representatives of the people must have control when this war is over. If that is not to be so, we should know it now. If our boys are not to have fought in vain for this democracy which we have envisaged, then we must make some move to be sure that our democracy is not simply a hollow sham when the crisis actually arrives. I suggest that not only in Canada but throughout the united

nations, as the representatives of the ordinary people in our own nation and perhaps also in an indirect way representing a cross-section of those in other nations, we have a right in time of war as in time of peace to see to it that these international combines and cartels are in our hands and that we are not in theirs. That seems to be at least a reasonable position for us to take in times like these.
I have no desire to attempt to arouse or inflame public opinion or to engender bitterness throughout our nation in time of war; that would be a despicable position for anyone to take, but I am serious about this matter, because as one of the representatives of the people I am alarmed at the situation in which we may find ourselves when this war is over unless we take some measures now. The united nations have shown in other respects that they can cooperate in a time of war, and that they can cooperate in their discussion of post-war problems. This looks to me like one of the major post-war problems we shall have to face.
In conclusion I suggest that the minister consider at once the question of appointing a royal commission to deal with all matters affecting this company, and other companies which may be similarly involved in worldwide international ramifications, which on the surface at least would seem to be inimical to the best interests of the ordinary man or woman. I would ask that he consider the whole question of such a royal commission, and that as a member of the government he, with the Prime Minister, should take the initiative in investigating the international arrangements and agreements under which a body such as that to which I referred a few minutes ago might be set up in the interests of a continuation of democracy and freedom in the years which lie ahead. Having made those investigations, I suggest that a move be made ait once toward renegotiating the contract in the light of what will then actually be found.
I make these observations with as much earnestness as any I have made since I entered public life, because I feel keenly and deeply that we as a parliament are not taking the steps necessary to ensure the kind of democracy that the fighting forces of Canada and of other countries who are engaged in the war effort will expect. I believe we are not taking the steps or providing the measures from which a true and a full democracy, a democracy which will make the world safe for the common man, and give him freedom of opportunity when the war is over, may be developed.

War Appropriation-Supplies

Mr. Chairman, the house
leader of the Progressive Conservative party has made an eloquent speech by using the device of setting up a straw man and then proceeding to demolish it. He has asked me one or two questions, and I should like to ask him one. If he found that one company was making all the aluminum that was made by the allied countries at the outbreak of the war, or prior to the outbreak of the war, would he refuse to do business with it at a time when the production of aluminum meant the salvation of the British empire, for the reason that the interests of that company were spread over more than one country?
The production of aluminum' is necessarily a business that involves more than one country. It is impossible to manufacture aluminum out of the resources of Canada alone. The principal raw material is bauxite, which comes from British Guiana. There has been an intense search in other areas for bauxite, but only a very small' and low-grade bauxite deposit has been found in the western United States. It is being used with the south American bauxite to the extent that it can be used with that product, in order to relieve the hazardous procedure of bringing bauxite from British Guiana through the submarine infested Caribbean to Canada. It has been found, however, that it is impossible to do without a large proportion of south American 'bauxite in the manufacture of Canadian aluminum. The next most important ingredient is cryolite, which comes from Greenland. Without that cryolite the manufacture of aluminum by present processes is impossible. Another ingredient in a form suited to the manufacturing of aluminum is found in Newfoundland-, and must be brought from Newfoundland to Canada to be used in our production.
I have mentioned only three of the chief elements which must come to Canada from other countries. There are other ingredients which are brought in, and necessarily so. From the outset Canada offers for the manufacture of aluminum from within Canada, first, hydroelectric power, which is essential, and second, efficient labour. The hydro-electric power and the efficient labour have resulted in the great industry on the Saguenay river. The use of the water powers which generate hydro-electric power does not involve any depletion of Canada's resources. Water has been flowing over the cliffs of the Saguenay for many hundreds of years, and will continue to do so, whether or not it is developed into w-ater power.
So far as labour is concerned, the second resource supplied by Canada, I would say that through the industry on the Saguenay a great community has been built where no community existed before the coming of the Aluminum company. It would be well worth the time of any hon. member to take a trip through the Saguenay country, and the lake St. John country, and see the homes and the agricultural development which has resulted from the activities of the Aluminum' company in that area. I believe it will be exceedingly difficult to say that the operations of the Aluminum company within Canada 'have left Canada a poorer nation, or one lower in the social scale than it would have been had that industry not located here.
A fallacy has been built up that huge profits are being made out of the war by the Aluminum company. I think if the last three ciphers can be struck off the capital invested in Canada by the Aluminum company through the years, and the last three ciphers struck from the gross and net profits of that company, it will be found that the returns both as to gross and- net profits are reasonable in proportion to the invested capital. If that is not so, and when we can stop making demands on the Aluminum company for new capital facilities and new expansion in Canada, in British Guiana and in other countries where operations of direct concern to the Canadian production are taking place, then I think we can go to the Aluminum company and ask for a renegotiation of the contract. But unless we find that there is an excessive profit, as measured by a percentage of capital invested in the enterprise, there is no purpose in the Department of Munitions and Supply attempting to force a renegotiated price.
The price of aluminum is one of the few prices which have been reduced in the war years. Someone has said that aluminum was being sold at a lower price in 1911. I wish that same gentleman would tell me of some other article that was not sold at a lower price in 1911 than it is being sold in this year 1943. Aluminum is distinctive I believe, through the fact that while it has been expanding its production enormously, building new capital facilities for the purpose, and building a great power development, the price has been lower in each year of this war than it was in the preceding year.
My hon. friend has set up another straw man when he says that the Aluminum company is not subject to the laws of Canada. I should like him to tell me upon what he bases that information. Aluminium Limited is a creature of the Dominion of Canada.
I did not say that.

The hon. member said that he wanted an international commission to deal with a subject that could not be dealt with by the Canadian government.

I know the minister
does not want to misinterpret my remarks. The reason I suggested an international commission, as the minister well knows, was the indication by the minister of his helplessness with respect to the whole question of international combinations. Have we full power to deal with the question of international combinations?
Quite.
Our responsibility then becomes that much greater.

The ownership of .properties in other countries does not create an international cartel. Is the Singer Sewing Machine company an international cartel? It owns a plant in almost every country in the world. So far as I know, that company is subject to the laws of the United States, just as Aluminium Limited is subject to the laws of Canada. There is no need of an international commission to deal with Aluminium Limited or with the Aluminum Company of Canada- they are both subject to the laws of Canada. Their properties within the dominion are subject to the jurisdiction of the federal government in the case of real property and to the jurisdiction of the provincial governments in the case of water powers.
Why was it necessary to conduct a prosecution of this company under the Sherman anti-trust laws of the United States?

This company was never prosecuted under the Sherman act of the United States; the company prosecuted was Alcoa, the Aluminum Company of America.
I was definite in my statement and said that that company was prosecuted by the country in which it has its head office. H the government of Canada wishes to start a similar prosecution against either Aluminium Limited or the Aluminum Company,of Canada, that is a matter wholly within its jurisdiction. These companies are domiciled in Canada, and are subject in every way to Canadian law.
Aluminium Limited was established here to escape the United States laws.
Nevertheless it is established here, and it is subject to Canadian laws and to Canadian courts.
Quite right.
I am discussing the subject matter of the speech by the leader in the House of Commons of the great Progressive Conservative party. He seems to be leading his party into strange doctrines.

The result is that an expansion is taking place in the United States, and necessarily so, to meet war requirements. I may be entirely in error, but my judgment is that it is better at this time to concentrate on obtaining aluminum to build aeroplanes to win the war -I think it would be utter madness to start a battle between the government of Canada and our Canadian producer of aluminum. The leader in this house of the Progressive Conservative party apparently would stop the war to start a prosecution.

withdraw that statement. I know he did not *make it intentionally, otherwise it might be more difficult to handle. I know he never thought for a moment that I said that. I did not suggest it, by inference, by implication or otherwise.

What did the hon. member say? I will read it to-morrow in Hansard.

The minister may not have been paying as close attention to what I was saying as he usually does. I suggested that in view of the allegations which have been made in connection with this company a royal commission should be appointed to inquire into these international cartels and to find out whether this company actually formed part of such a cartel. In addition there should be a renegotiation of the contract in the light of the circumstances which have been brought to light. I went a little further and suggested that as this was an international situation, Canada should give a lead and set up an international body which would attempt to solve some of the difficulties which have been mentioned in this debate.

In reply to my hon. friend's suggestion, may I say that I have pointed out that Aluminium Limited owns plants in a number of countries, and necessarily so if it is going to obtain the various products that go to making finished aluminum here in Canada. I know it to be a fact that the personnel of Aluminium Limited comprise all the men who are experienced in the art of making aluminum. This happens to be the only company that is making aluminum in this country. As one who must provide aluminum for our war effort, I would not want to take the responsibility of taking the attention of the executives of Aluminium Limited from their task of making aluminum. I would not want to place them in the witness box at this time to tell about their pre-war business dealings.
Another Bren gun inquiry.

I do not think this is the time for that kind of investigation. Aluminium Limited will be here after the war. If at that time it is felt that their proceedings were improper, they can be investigated.. The
Aluminum company, along with other citizens of Canada, have done their utmost to meet the requirements of the allies in the field in which they are expert. I have said it before and I say it again, that they have stretched their resources to the utmost in order to do a job in the winning of the war. It only needed a suggestion to be made that we must have more aluminum, that we believed that they were capable of doing more, to have them increase their production. There has been a singleness of purpose in the conduct of their business which I think could be taken as an example by any other industry in this country. As I say, this department is aware of their operating position; their company accounts are an open book; a firm of auditors audits the books, and the results of those audits are known to the department of munitions.
What is the firm?
Price, Waterhouse and Company.
Is not that the firm of audiors usually employed by the corporation itself?

I think so, but it is a responsible firm of auditors which operates in every British country and in the United States as well. Audits are made of the accounts of the company, the expenditures are known to the government, and we do not believe that the profits are excessive. If a few ciphers could be struck off the figures, and they were compared with the accounts of any other company doing business in this war, it would be found, I think, that the gross and net profits of this company are not excessive.
Have our own cost accountants investigated the cost of producing this product-investigated, for instance, the cost of labour and materials?
We have all the cost accountants we can get, but if we put them all on that operation it would take the rest of the war perhaps'' to follow through.
Could not our own cost accountants check over the figures?

I am quite prepared to take the cost accounting of Price, Waterhouse and Company. I think most business concerns in the world have done that at one time or another, and I am prepared to do it. I think their cost accounting is to be relied on. The reason we have not renegotiated the Aluminum company contracts is that we have seen no necessity for doing so from the figures

Mr. Chairman, the
whole discussion up to the present time has been very interesting to me and highly instructive. I have enjoyed every moment of it. I enjoyed the speech of the leader of the Progressive Conservative party. I enjoyed too the reference he made to the fine spirit of optimism which prevailed in the convention out in Winnipeg, as a result of which his party proposes to find jobs for everyone. But I do wish that somewhere, somehow the party had taken pains to indicate the technique by which they are going to find those jobs.

Hear, hear-as in
1930!

That technique was altogether missing. If I have failed to see it I hope that one of my Progressive Conservative friends will call around and give me the authorities on the matter. I should like to know where they propose to find markets, and how they propose to guarantee markets, and how they propose to guarantee prices. I am going to tell the Progressive Conservatives here and now that unless they can find adequate markets for the production of Canadian industry they cannot put men to work, because work depends primarily and naturally upon work in industry, and industry depends upon the amount of goods that industry can sell. If industries cannot sell goods they cannot run, and if they cannot run they cannot employ men. Once the Progressive Conservatives get that thoroughly embedded in their thinking they will really begin to be progressive.
And the Liberals too.

And the Liberals too will have something to look forward to. But where are they going to get the money to increase the purchasing power of the people to enable the people to purchase the goods which industry stands ready to produce? Are they going to raise it by taxation and by borrowing? If they are, then I might as well tell them they can give up now and save themselves a whole lot of trouble in a fruitless search. If they cannot find enough money to put into the hands of the people to give the people purchasing power with which to purchase the production of industry, which production industry is finding a market for now in this war, they will have fewer markets, less production and less work. The laws governing these facts are as irrevocable as the laws

of the Medes and Persians, only more so. I just thought that I should like to say that in respect to the Progressive Conservatives. I have no quarrel with them. I am just earnestly trying to find a solution, because I have sons and daughters and grandsons and granddaughters growing up in this country and I should like to see matters so arranged before I die that there is a chance for them all to find work if they want to work and make a living and build homes. But I have not found anything coming from the Progressive Conservatives or from the Liberals which has indicated how this is to be achieved.
With respect to the monopolies referred to by the leader of the opposition and by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, I had not intended to refer to them, but inasmuch as they have been brought up I shall do so. How do monopolies develop in this country? How can they be controlled? Why is it that we do not now control monopolies? Is it that we do not possess the power to make laws, or is it that we do not possess the power of money over these monopolies? The answer to the second question is yes. We can make the laws all right in this country, and we can have the courts enforce them, but up to the present time we have not established unchallengeable control over money. We do not find ourselves able to control private industry-and money is the secret. I should like to know what the leader of the Progressive Conservatives would do in order to control these great monopolies after his international commission had discovered them.
I wish to turn for a minute or two to the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and to give him just an idea of how I reacted to his excellent speech. I think that last night he did the finest job he ever did in parliament. It was splendid, ably delivered. I enjoyed listening to him. He told us all about the evil which exists, but he did not indicate how he himself would solve the problem which was presented by that evil.

If there was a supranational government established, it would control not only our aluminum but every other industry; it would control all the business of this country and everything else in this country. We should be unable to establish any kind of control over it-which is a very serious matter and which has much importance in connection with the fine remarks of the leader of the Progressive Conservatives. I want to point out to him that I am not opposing but agreeing entirely with his remarks about democracy. If Canada cannot be mistress in her own home and) her own house, she cannot have democracy.
I must have been right on that occasion.

Oh, the hon. member is right; everything he said was right. I am only finding fault with the things he left unsaid, and they are very important.
I wish to turn now for a few moments to the minister's remarks. I thought he gave a statement which impressed the whole country. I do not know when there has been a more striking and more valuable speech delivered in this chamber. I fancy that Canadians generally could hardly believe that their youthful Canada, which not long ago was called playfully "Jack Canuck", was capable of such
tremendous and varied production. The minister went so far as to use the following words, as reported in Hansard, page 3556:
Never again will there be any doubt that Canada can manufacture anything that can be manufactured elsewhere.
Every drop of Canadian blood in my body just leaped, every drop of British blood in me just raced with joy, when I read that. If Canada can produce anything that can be produced anywhere, is there any reason why Canada oannot stand completely independent and have absolute democracy and be completely mistress in her own home? None whatever; only the failure of Canadians to know how to manage the whole situation. I thought, when the minister gave his imposing array of accomplishments, what a triumph for individual enterprise! That much of the production has been a result of government cooperation we will grant, but in the main, by and large, it has been the result of private enterprise. There was no need of taking away private control, of socialization and all that kind of thing, in order to get production-and production is primarily what we need in any country in order that we may have a high standard of living.
Now, if Canada can produce the things she needs-and I am sure she can; scientific progress is proving ever more conclusively that she can-is there any reason why she should not do it? I have contended in this house ever since I came here that Canada should be producing her own sugar, and should have done so; and one of the gravest errors this government made was the failure to provide for the manufacture of Canada's complete sugar supply. I say that that will stand as a reflection on the government and as evidence, to the end of time, wherever it is known, of their lack of wisdom and judgment. We should produce our requirements of everything else that we can produce. If we produce what we can consume we can be more and more self-sufficient. And why not?
In the course of the debate on this three billion dollar war appropriation we have had a long talking time. If I remember correctly, we commenced the discussion of this appropriation on May 13. I have listened with great interest and thoughtfulness to most of the speeches which 'have been delivered, and I have asked myself this question, "Is this speech a 'wasting of time?" And I must confess that it is next to impossible to say of any speech which I have heard in the house that it has been wasting time. It has been good; and yet we have used much time, time that we needed for other things. Now we hear talk and read

in the newspaper rumours about closing up in the middle of July. I do not know of anything that could strike consternation into the people of Canada more surely than if they understood all that this house has to take care of this year and it is then reported that the house would rush and scramble and tear in order to get through in the middle of July, or would leave undone the things it ought to do because it has not time to deal with them.
