In a general way I would say that parliament must somehow reform itself. I do not know just how it should be done; I am not prepared to make a suggestion now; but certainly parliament must bring itself up to date. Ox-cart ideas and horse and buggy methods are not good enough for this streamlined high-powered age, and our achievement this year has clearly shown it. Parliament has clung too long to out of date ideas and antiquated methods. Parliament has shown thereby a dangerous lack of vision, and "where there is no vision the people perish." Both democracy and the people are in grave danger at the present moment of perishing-not in Canada alone, but on the American continent. Dangers are lurking on every hand, both within the nation and without. We members of parliament must be exceedingly vigilant and resourceful if we are to be equal to the demands made upon us in this day and generation.
This is the eighty-ninth day of the fourth session of the nineteenth parliament. In the main, hon. members have spoken freely; that is, we have free speech. But on the whole they have failed to achieve their desired objectives [DOT]-and I would include in that expression every member in the house. All I need to do is to refer to the old age pension question as an example. I think there is not an hon. member who does not want the aged people to receive $30 a month and receive it right away-not only the ones who are now receiving pensions, but everyone who has arrived at sixty years of age. Why are the members not able to attain their desire? There is something radically wrong; that simple little illustration proves it beyond the shadow of a doubt. When not only the whole of the people of Canada want a thing but all members of parliament want it, and we call this country a democracy, and still we cannot get it, then surely something is wrong. Where could I find more complete jutsification for the remarks I have just made? In other words, ideas and 
methods which we have had in this house up to the.present time as a whole have just not got us anywhere; they have not got us where we know we ought to be.
It is not so much that hon. members do not have freedom of speech, but that somehow they lack wisdom to use that freedom of speech effectively by translating it into action. True, we have prosecuted world war number two with a gratifying measure of success. But with the great underlying causes which brought on that war, this parliament has not once come to grips-not once-in all the seven years I have been here. I maintain that that, again, is a condemnation of this house, somehow, somewhere. This parliament ought to ascertain without further delay the causes which brought on this war. Surely they are to be found, and surely hon. members will agree about them when they are found. This parliament should face the facts fairly and fearlessly. It ought to find means of removing these causes once and for all, and it should seek to do so diligently and systematically, without passion or prejudice. The members now sitting here ought to see to it that every possible effort is made to remove the causes of war. Failure to ascertain the causes of this war, failure to find the remedy, and neglect to apply that remedy, will mean that this parliament will become guilty of criminal negligence in the highest degree and will stand condemned before generations yet to come. And the members now sitting here, in this year of Our Lord 1943, will betray their trust, will betray the people who elected them, will betray the boys and girls who fight, will betray the millions of workers who toil, will betray the babes in the people's homes, and the generations yet unborn. This parliament cannot escape responsibility. Its duty is to act now in the coming months of 1943.
There are several important matters that this House of Commons should deal with itself. Members will ask, how are we to do it? If the members of all parties, in an honest, straightforward endeavour, tried to do it they could do it; perhaps not in this house, but in this city, in this building. The great question is, Do we want to do it? The greater question is, Are we going to be honourable enough to do it? For example, we could determine as a group of members outside the house entirely, and independently of party lines, that we will find the truth and the whole truth and act upon it at once. We do not agree on it among ourselves in parliament, but outside, in the main, we do. What is the matter? We could appoint non-partisan committees to find the truth; and we could hear the truth in secret

War Appropriation-Supplies
sessions if needs be; and then, if we unitedly insisted, suitable action could be taken and we could get results in this house, this year.
Among the problems that could and should be considered and dealt with, with satisfying thoroughness, the following might be listed: First, the treaty of peace. In the last war we fought right through, and no one seemed to have any idea what kind of peace we were to have. All we heard was that we were fighting to make the world safe for democracy and fighting a war to end wars; but just as we find to-day, not a person seemed to trouble himself about the question, how are we to do it? No one seems ever to trouble now about that question,-how is it to be done?
We should know what Canada's war aims are. I challenge any hon. member to rise in his place or to tell me outside that he knows what Canada's war aims are. Is that not a sad state of affairs? Then we should know what the various proposals are that are made in secret dispatches. Unquestionably it has been mentioned that certain proposals have been made. Why should we not know what they are? We are the members of parliament elected by the sovereign people of Canada in a democratic election. What an insult to our intelligence that we are forbidden to know these things! We should know them and should know exactly the difficulties in the way.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar did the country a service yesterday when he exposed) this aluminum company and gave the details. No matter whether there is anything wrong that cannot be righted; he gave us the truth and we ought to know the truth. We ought to know what the truth is in regard to all these, things-such truths as the following one, for instance, which has astonished me! Somebody from Canada went around in 1937 and committed Canada to the undertaking that she would not increase her sugar beet acreage, that she would not do anything to increase it. No one in this parliament knew about that. That man made an agreement which has injured the people of this country incalculably during this war. Who was he and who told* him he could go and do it, and why was it that this country, which never heard about it, was bound by the agreement? And there must be many other agreements similar to that. This house should know them, every one of them.
We ought to know what is involved in the united nations' idea. Listen to the words as they are pronounced over the radio-united
nations. Well, now, what is involved in these united nations? We ought to know in detail so that everyone might understand. What are the proposals of these men who are working behind the scenes? How was it that at the Hot Springs conference Roosevelt tethered the press a safe distance from the conference? How was it that Morgenthau was so much annoyed when it leaked out in London that he had an international currency stabilization programme? Why was that? Am I to be told that the members of this house, in this responsible position, in this great country of ours with all its future before it, are not entitled to know these things? Have we lost the independence and courage of our fathers, that independence and courage which made magna charta a possibility? Are we afraid to be worthy to hold the positions we now occupy? We ought to know what is involved in this food conference. Every once in a while, through some speech made in some room in the Chateau Laurier or some assembly room of the House of Commons, some little thing leaks out that indicates that a good many things are contemplated with which members of this house do not agree, and yet it is all done in the dark somewhere, with the press tethered away -the press and parliament tethered. It is not in the public interest that we should know! We are immature, a species of glorified moron, I presume!
Not glorified.

Not even glorified. We ought to know what is involved in the Atlantic charter. There has been talk, profuse talk about the Atlantic charter-how we are to guarantee freedom from want and freedom from fear-with never a word about how it is to be done, who is to pay the cost of it, where the money is to come from. Never a word. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that is a most singular state of affairs. I want to know whether the members of this house, particularly in the Liberal party, intend to submit to that kind of thing. I wonder if they are sufficiently docile lambs to take that all the time lying down, all of them.
I think they are.

We ought to know what share Canada is to contribute to this guarantee of freedom from want. Are we to have a mutual aid bill perpetuated through the years? If we are, how big will it be; will it be a billion dollars or two billion dollars, or will it be more; what do we intend to supply through that mutual aid bill, and how is it to be financed? I am surprised that I have never
War Appropriation-Supplies

seen that question asked and answered in the press of our land; that is something which astonishes me. Canada certainly ought to know what her share in this glorious enterprise is to be; if she is to participate. Are we to have a lease-lend for Canada? Is the United States to be able to perpetuate the lease-lend arrangement for twenty, thirty or forty years; is her lease-lend arrangement to depend upon the particular administration that happens to be in power, so that if by chance everything should be operating nicely under President Roosevelt and he should be eliminated from the scene in time, the lease-lend arrangement will be cancelled, and the people who thought they were guaranteed against want will find themselves at loose ends, as they were before the present war? Is that to be the arrangement; and, if so, are we, as members of this house, to submit to anything as insecure as that? Yet I do not see any evidence that we are to learn the truth about it; I say we ought to learn the truth before we leave this house.
The other day I read a statement by President Roosevelt, and I have read1 two or three similar statements, to the effect that the first thing to be done is for each nation to set its own house in order. With that I completely agree. Surely we ought to set our own house in order, but we cannot do that unless we have certain powers. We must have unchallengeable control of our currency and credit, of our production and of our price structure; we must have complete control of our own markets within our own country. If we cannot have these powers we cannot set our house in order. Yet practically all the supranational government schemes propose to take away from us each and every one of those powers, in greater or less degree, so far as I have read accounts of them. Every single hon. member should understand that fully. We could use the empire parliamentary association. Far be it from me to cast any reflection upon the empire parliamentary association, but I must say that I have been deeply disappointed in the amount of real learning we have obtained from that association. I do not see why we should not bring it really to life. I do not see why we should not arrange study clubs in which we might hear the truth from all sides, instead of having a lecture by some-I was going to say "emaciated"-relic of the League of Nations, who comes and tells us his idea and goes his way, making place for someone else to come along and tell us the same thing at another time. I am becoming entirely fed up when I think that all the speeches over the radio, all the speeches in these clubs and that sort of thing are along the same line, and all strangely resemble the propaganda which Sir 
William Beveridge apparently was sent or brought to this country to carry on. I am suspicious in the highest degree. I would say that not only should we learn through the empire parliamentary association or through some other dependable means, but we should -be able to take our knowledge to the remotest parts of Canada, to every constituency, so that the people may share it.
I think it is time this house faced up squarely to the problem of what we intend to do about our national debt after this war is over. I have gathered the impression that hon. members just look upon this as a very touchy question and steer clear of it as something they would rather not face. Are we not aware that the boys and girls who are now fighting our war and who will sit in this chamber twenty years from now will have to face this problem, that they will not be able to leave it alone? What sort of people are we, who are supposed to be taking care of their interests, when we are so neglectful of this vital matter?
It is also time we know what we intend to do about the unemployment situation after this war. I read the other day that it was estimated by rather responsible men in the United States that shortly after the conclusion of the war there would be twenty million unemployed in that country. If the number of unemployed in Canada is in relation to that figure, is it not high time every member of this house was exercising himself with the deepest concern in regard to this matter? How are we to handle our tax structure? I am positively alarmed when I talk with people who are in the grip of the tyrannical tax structure which has been imposed upon the people of this country; it is merciless, implacable, immovable, inescapable, crushing, devastating, disheartening; it is a horrible thing, but there is no evidence whatever that it will be relaxed in any degree at all after this war is over. Yet we members sit here supinely doing nothing about it, only piling up the debt so that the structure may bear upon the people with even greater severity.
Another important matter that must be considered in connection with this debate, and one which I thought of raising several times, is the question of what we shall do with our armed forces after the war is over. As the minister for naval services was talking about his superb navy, the thought ran through my mind: Are we to have that superb navy after the war, and is everyone in Canada to be taught that it is necessary? Will parliament cheerfully vote the supply, year after year, to support that navy, or shall we have people here like those bewildered creatures who sat

War Appropriation-Supplies
here in 1937 and moved that every estimate be reduced to $1, who kept up their propaganda until they fooled the people of Canada into believing that we did not need any defences? That is important to know, whether we are to have a strong navy, a strong army and a strong air force after the war, because if we are to have a strong navy and army we will build for permanence. Not only will we construct the buildings; we will build the concept in the minds of the people, so that they will know, and they will be careful not to send to this parliament people who do not know that we must have a good strong army, navy and air force to be able to defend ourselves. Are we to have strong defence forces, or are they to fall into decay?
Then let us go on and ask ourselves this question not only with respect to Canada but with respect to the British commonwealth. During the period following the Napoleonic wars until the outbreak of the first great war the world witnessed one of the most peaceful eras in its history. There may have been many small wars, but there was nothing like the conflagration that burnt out at the beginning and at the end of that century. Why was that? Those who are fairly well informed tell me that there was established what is know as the pax Britannica, the British peace, because -the British people were strong enough to maintain peace. Are we now prepared to build up a British commonwealth organization, a cooperative arrangement, as a result of which we can have once more something similar to a pax Britannica? That is something that has worked successfully already. We ought to know about -this possibility, but as a whole we do not know a thing about it. We have not done any constructive thinking or talking on it in this house.
Then the matter of social security ought to be taken care of by -this house. We have heard the Beveridge scheme. By the confession of Sir William Beveridge himself, if I gathered it aright, his scheme is impossible and useless unless two things are guaranteed: first, full employment; second, a stable and equitable price structure. If we could guarantee employment and a stable and equitable price structure in Canada we would need no Beveridge plan. The big problem facing this house and this country is how to establish complete employment and a stable and equitable price structure throughout the country. That was the problem facing the Progressive Conservatives when they met. Strange that so many people overlook these things! Strange that so many of these newspapers which watch with almost malignant
scrutiny the words of members -of this house, in order to pounce upon them and write offensive editorials about them, have not noticed the discrepancy in the Beveridge report, and commented upon it! Never a word! Is there a mutual agreement to leave these things alone?
Another matter which ought to be taken up before the house continues its deliberations for another week is that of the sufferers who are at present enduring hardships that are a disgrace to the country.. I have already referred to the old age pensioners. Let me now refer to the war veterans of the last war, and the widows of war veterans. They are now growing old and are rapidly diminishing in number, but they still suffer cruelly, while the representatives they have sent to Ottawa somehow or another seem to forget them-seem to forget everything, except to talk.
Perhaps the most imminent danger which confronts us at the present time is the idea of supranational government, to which I have already referred. Its advocates and their disciples always urge that supra-national government will prevent war, but they never show how it will be done. I say supranational government may try to prevent war, but it will render universal rebellion inevitable-rebellion with civil strife and bloodshed and famine over the fair stretches of Canada and the United States.
Every scheme of supranational government I have read about-and I have read all I could get my hands on-embodies international control of credit and currency. There is much talk about the control of production, the lowering of tariff barriers and other restrictions to trade. Somehow or another the men who talk about world problems do not take the trouble to point out why tariff restrictions are erected by weak nations, and why they impose exchange control. These men rarely explain that nations imposing trade restrictions do so in an- endeavour to improve their economy, because they fall behind in the -contest for trade, and therefore have an adverse trade balance. And of course the advocates of supranational government never talk about the existence of such a cause. They never mention the remedy except in most general terms-beautiful, high-sounding words, which, somehow or another seem to mesmerize many people.
Supranational government can be avoided with -all its dangers. May I read -a statement which hon. members will find in the Ottawa Citizen of January 11, 1943, on the back page under the heading "Plan For Permanent Peace." This is a criticism of a book by
War Appropriation-Supplies

Doctor Hans Heymann. Strange how so many of these German names get into the books having to do with this supranational plan. It is an astonishing thing; I cannot quite understand it. It reminds me very much of those international financiers. The article quoted from the London Chamber oj Commerce Journal explains that the idea conveyed by the whole book is of a world bank. "But Doctor Heymann is a financial expert and all his ideas on post-war reconstruction find their inevitable culmination in a 'huge new international banking mechanism'-a world bank to create money and credit." . . . "While nations may agree to some limitation of their sovereignty in respect of their external affairs, any proposal which involves interference with-much less control of-their internal affairs, as Doctor Heymann's scheme does, would mean the abandonment of the most important of President Roosevelt's four freedoms, freedom from fear. Currency and credit are the master keys to the economic and social life of any community, and for a nation to be asked to hand those keys to a clique of international bankers is calculated to strike terror into the hearts of millions who are facing death to preserve their right to manage their own affairs."

speechtext: The hon. member has spoken forty minutes.
I shall take another occasion to finish my speech, in case hon. members do not wish to hear the rest of it now.

I was surprised this afternoon at the complacency and confidence with which the minister came to the defence of the aluminum interests, and the complacency with which he passed over the suggestion that the situation warranted an investigation of some kind. I was surprised furthermore yesterday by the readiness of the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) to admit the inability of the government to deal with this international cartel.
Hon. members who spoke on this subject yesterday dealt with the international side of aluminum development, and the monopolistic control which had been effected in the development of aluminum. There is another monopoly which to my mind is far more serious to the people of Canada than that affecting aluminum. I refer to the monopoly of electric power which this great company has attained in Canada. I am confident there is not an hon. member in the house, regardless of his political affiliations, regardless of what he thinks of private ownership versus public ownership, who does not recognize the danger 
to public interests and the danger to industr" in this country that lies in permitting any monopoly of our water power. That power is the very lifeblood of industry, and any monopolistic enterprise which can gain control of the right to develop power from the water that flows in our rivers has gained a stranglehold on the very industry of our country.
I doubt that there is an hon. member who is not convinced that any monopoly by any privately-owned company of the sole right to develop power from our rivers, and to distribute that power, is inimical to the public interests of our country.
In his speech yesterday the minister said:
It has been suggested that this development-
He was speaking of Shipshaw.
[DOT]-was carried out to block the St. Lawrence development. Let me remind hon. members that Canada is committed to the St. Lawrence development; that it has agreed with the United States to proceed with that development, and the St. Lawrence development was blocked not in Canada but in the United States.
I am not as confident as the minister of the truth of the statement that the St. Lawrence development was blocked not in Canada but in the United States. I want to show to the committee this afternoon that the recent development of Shipshaw marks the successful culmination of a long series of attempts on the part of the aluminum interests to perfect an international pool of power which would not only keep competing aluminum companies out of the field, but would render the state of New York and the provinces of Ontario and Quebec almost entirely dependent on power from their development in Quebec, for their supply of the very lifeblood of modern' civilization.
This battle for power control and for the establishment of an international pool of power has been carried on for more than twenty years by lobbying, by litigation, by the organization of holding companies and trusts, and by every means that such a powerful corporation could use. For more than twenty years the aluminum interests have sought, first, to get control of the St. Lawrence water project; second, failing that, to obstruct its development as a publicly-owned enterprise and, third, to carry out in the meantime a policy of encirclement, whereby it could get control of all other available power and thereby preempt the power market. By successfully obstructing the development of the St. Lawrence project the aluminum interests have rendered it necessary for New York state, the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec to enter into contracts with private companies, practically every one of

War Appropriation-Supplies
which is tied up directly or indirectly with the aluminum interests. In this connection let me quote the periodical PM of May 23, 1943. An article, dated Washington, reads:
The Shipshaw power project on the Saguenay river in Quebec was envisioned by Aluminum Company of America (Alcoa) as far back as 1925 as a means of preventing public development of the St. Lawrence.
Documents and testimony on file in the federal district court here in the government's antitrust suit against Alcoa disclose that:
Alcoa bought the Saguenay river power sites, including Shipshaw, from the Duke-Price interests in 1925 and 1926, after it learned that they had planned to use this power to manufacture aluminum in Quebec in competition with Alcoa.
So anxious was Alcoa to prevent this that it paid $40,000,000 for these power sites, then largely undeveloped. The province of Quebec had sold these sites a quarter century earlier for $40,000.
On the eve of the purchase in 1925, Arthur V. Davis, chairman and directing genius of Alcoa, sent Alcoa's chief hydraulic engineer, James W. Rickey, to make a survey of the Saguenay properties.
Rickey at that time outlined the possibilities of the Shipshaw power development, a second "Boulder Dam," construction of which has now been financed for Alcoa by the American, Canadian, British and Australian governments.
Alcoa's chief engineer saw Shipshaw's huge power possibilities as a means of so "encircling" the St. Lawrence project that it could be developed only on Alcoa's terms or by Alcoa.
The plan was to use Shipshaw power to "sew up" these areas in which St. Lawrence power would have to be sold: Montreal, Ontario, upstate New York.
It was hoped thereby not only to prevent public development of the St. Lawrence, by preempting the markets for its power, but also to block further public power projects by Ontario's great publicly owned hydro electric.
_ In pursuance of this grand strategy, Alcoa in July, 1925, acquired the Chute 5 Caron and Shipshaw sites; and in May, 1926, the rest of the Saguenay power sites and properties.
Conferences looking toward disposal of this power, when developed, were held by Leighton G. McCarthy, then Alcoa's Canadian counsel now Canada's minister to Washington, with two key Canadian figures.

I said I was reading from PM of Sunday, May 23.

The article continues :
The basic strategy for these moves is outlined in a ten-page letter and report which Rickey sent on February 25, 1925, to Arthur V. Davis, then vacationing in Palm Beach.
"If this scheme could be put through," Rickey reported to his chief, "decision regarding the St. Lawrence development is of secondary importance, but when agreement is finally reached we would occupy a very strong and strategic position."
The very nature of the St. Lawrence poweT and waterway project lends itself to the purposes which the aluminum company have set

War Appropriation-Supplies

out to achieve. The project requires the ratification of agreements in which five governments are involved. For twenty years the company has been able to provide obstructions to the project by working through one or more of these governments and committees or boards set up to work out the agreements. Let us review a few of the high lights of the tactics they have used to achieve their full purpose of securing, first, control of St. Lawrence power; second, the obstruction of the development of St. Lawrence power by government and, third, the gaining of control of other available sources of power. I shall not weary the committee with the long and involved story of how since the beginning of this century the aluminum interests have persistently and successfully gained control of the production and distribution of electric power in the Niagara and St. Lawrence areas or the details of the story of their obstructing the development of power by public ownership. I shall touch on only a few of the high lights.
The company later known as the Aluminum Company of America was first organized in the state of Pennsylvania in 1889. Its name was changed in 1907 to the Aluminum Company of America. In that year it set up a holding company, in which it held 100 per cent of the capital stock, for the purpose of securing power sites. It became interested in the Niagara power when that power was first converted from hydraulic power to hydro-electric at the turn of the century. It then entered into an agreement with the Niagara Falls Power company by which it attached its own generators to the company's plant and by which that company agreed not to sell power to any other company producing aluminum. It has from that time to this been the largest purchaser of power from the Niagara Falls Power company.
Let me give one little incident. That company, so closely associated with aluminum has fought through the courts of the United States for years to get authority to divert the entire United States share of power at Niagara Falls. It has carried on litigation over the years to secure that diversion and was only finally stopped by judgment given in the United States court of appeals on December 2, 1942.
At the time the company's name was changed to the Aluminum Company of America back in 1907, it organized a company known as the Long Sault Development company-again a company entirely owned by Aluminum-for the purpose of damming the St. Lawrence at the Long Sault rapids. It got so far as to get legislation through the New York legislature, and then applied in 1907, and in 1909, 1911, and

1912 to get legislation through the congress of the United States. Canada was drawn into the picture, and the matter came several times before the Canadian government and the International Joint Commission. In all the discussions there were three men who were prominent, and whose names have been prominent right down through the years in connection with Aluminum's control of water power. They were: Leighton McCarthy, K.C., counsel at that time for the Long Sault Development company and the St. Lawrence Power company; T. W. Rickey, engineer for the Aluminum Company of America; and Arthur Y. Davis, president of Aluminum. That enterprise, that attempt to dam the St. Lawrence, was only blocked after years of litigation when the United States court of appeals in 1913 supported the repeal of the 1907 legislation. I should just like to read what Governor Alfred Smith of New York State had to say when speaking on this subject on February 1, 1926, as reported in the fifth annual report of the Power Authority of the State of New York for the year ended December 31, 1935. Governor Smith said:
The two great sources of hydro-electric energy are at Niagara falls and on the St. Lawrence river. Corporations eager to get control of these water powers have been working on the project for years. As far back as 1907, by special charter, the right to develop the St. Lawrence river was granted to the Long Sault Development Company, which special charter was repealed by the legislature of 1913. In no way discouraged during all the years that have passed, private corporations still have their eye on the great power possibilities of the St. Lawrence river. ... If both of these sources of supply fall into the hands of private companies, the possibility for future state development will be lost forever.
Arthur V. White, reporting to the Canadian Commission of Conservation in 1913, had this to say at page 13 of his report:
Back of the activities to secure control of all the water-power development, power transmission and other rights and privileges at, and in the vicinity of, the Long Sault rapids is the Aluminum Company of America, commonly known as the Aluminum Trust. Connected with the Aluminum company is the St. Lawrence Securities Company, a holding company through which provision was made for an issue of $1,550,000 of stock to provide funds:
"for the actual cost of improvements of the canal and other property of the St. Lawrence River Power Company, or the development of any water rights along the Little Sault owned or controlled."
The St. Lawrence Securities Company-
That was a holding company for Aluminum, and in which Aluminum held 100 per cent
of the stock.

I had hoped that my hon. friend would refer to the fact that the International Joint Commission had during the last war granted the Aluminum company the right to erect a barrier across the river, and they have never been able to get them to remove that barrier since that time.

Thank you. The Ontario Hydro Electric Commission became very much interested in 1920 in developing St. Lawrence power. Sir Adam Beck realized at that time that if Ontario's needs for power were to be met by publicly-owned plants it would be necessary to begin the development of the St. Lawrence power project before the Niagara power project was operated to its capacity. In 1921 the Ontario hydro electric commission submitted to the International Joint Commission an elaborate statement and an engineering report respecting the proposal to develop the St. Lawrence waterways. At the time the commission went on record as being in favour of proceeding with the development of the international section of the river first. That policy is in strange contrast with the policy adopted by the Ontario hydro electric commission some years later, after the Aluminum company had done their lobbying, as I shall show later in this speech.
Following this application in 1921, the Ontario hydro electric commission formally applied to the Canadian government for approval of its plans for the initial step in a two-stage development of the international section of the St. Lawrence river. Before making this formal request, in July, 1924, a delegation from more than 350 Ontario municipalities requested the dominion government
72537-232J
for early approval of the commission's plans. Unfortunately for the publicly-owned hydro system of Ontario, the aluminum interests at that time, in 1921 and 1922, had very influential friends at court in New York state. The governor of the day and the legislature of New York at the time were much more favourably inclined to private enterprise than to a publicly-owned enterprise. Legislation was granted permitting the Aluminum company and other companies to lease state-owned power sites for a long period of years, and between 1921 and 1926 application was made for twenty-two of those leases. A company owned outright by the Aluminum company was just on the point of getting its lease when Governor Alfred Smith was elected on the platform of a publicly-owned St. Lawrence system and was able to veto the lease which was just about to be issued to the Aluminum company's subsidiary. At the same time, in 1921, the Aluminum company joined forces with the General Electric Company and the du Pont interests, and they organized what was known as the Frontier Corporation. The Aluminum company maintained a controlling interest in that corporation. That corporation controlled all the privately-owned rights to power on the United States side of the St. Lawrence together with subsidiaries on the Canadian side at Niagara and Cornwall. I can give the committee the purpose of that corporation as it was given at an investigation held by order of the United States senate and reported in their document No. 72:
The Frontier Corporation was organized for the purpose of acquiring from Aluminum Co. of America, E. I. du Pont de Nemours & Co., and General Electric Co. certain lands, water rights, water privileges, and flowage rights on the St. Lawrence river in the towns of Massena, Louisville, and Waddington, N.Y.
It also acquired certain maps, surveys, and engineering data concerning the development of hydro-electric power along the St. Lawrence river.
It also acquired all of the issued outstanding capital stock of St. Lawrence Power Company, Ltd., an operating utility in Canada. It also acquired all of the authorizations to dam the St. Lawrence river, which might be granted to the Louisville Power Corporation or St. Lawrence Transmission Co., that company now being called the St. Lawrence Valley Power Corporation.
I have already indicated that the Aluminum company controlled the Frontier Corporation. That corporation was particularly interested in watching every move made by the Ontario hydro electric commission. This interest is evidenced by the activities of the corporation's legal counsel in Canada, Mr. Leighton McCarthy, throughout the years 1922 to 1926. During an inquiry which was held before the
War Appropriation-Supplies

Federal Trade Commission at Washington in 1934 there was presented to that commission certain accounts rendered by Mr. McCarthy to the Frontier Corporation. These were presented as exhibits. They were his accounts for his services performed in the interests of the corporation in Canada. They show clearly the Aluminum company's interest in Ontario hydro.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

When the committee rose at six o'clock, I was at the point of putting on the record a number of accounts rendered by Leighton McCarthy, K.C. to the Frontier corporation as evidence of that corporation's interest.in Ontario hydro.
The first of these accounts covers the period from October, 1921 to May 31, 1922, and is itemized as follows:
Fee to Mr. Leighton McCarthy, K.C., generally representing interests of corporation in Canada (including attendance before the International Joint Commission, interview with members of Canadian government and senate and Sir Adam Beck and reporting thereon. . . .
And further on:
Procuring statutes and regulations re water power and water privileges, forwarding same to Mr. Rickey, perusing and considering special report from Mr. Rickey regarding the meeting of International Joint Commission at Washington, preparing special report on the Canadian situation before the formation of Frontier Corporation.
The second covers the period from June 1, 1922 to May 31, 1923, and is itemized as follows:
Fee to Mr. Leighton McCarthy, K.C.. generally representing interests of corporation in Canada, including special interviews with members of Canadian government, Senate, House of Commons, Sir Adam Beck, and reporting thereon. . . .

Mr. Chairman, I suggest to you that this discussion is entirely out of order. The item under consideration is additions and extensions to plants, and not one dollar of the item has anything to do with the Aluminum Company of Canada. We never paid for extension of plant of the Aluminum Company of Canada. We simply had nothing to do with water powers, either the St. Lawrence or any other. So far as this item is concerned, we have paid not a dollar in assistance in the building of waterpower developments. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, if this discussion is relevant to the item?

On the point of order may I remind you, Mr. Chairman, that when the Minister of Munitions and Supply introduced this matter on Friday, in the very able review which he gave, he made reference to the expansion of the aluminum facilities and referred to it as the largest that he had, and he also made reference to the enlargement of water-power facilities at Shipshaw. In view of his reference to these two phases of industrial development, I submit that this discussion is in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has now spoken for over forty minutes.
Taking into consideration the interruptions, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have made allowance for the interruptions. The hon. gentleman was supposed to have until five minutes after eight, and I allowed him to continue until thirteen minutes after eight.

I wish to take only a few moments, because I have very little except constructive criticism to offer. I do wish, however, after having consulted the Speaker and the Clerk, to direct attention to statements made in an article appearing in the weekly newspaper known as the Montreal Standard last Sunday by one Austin Cross, headed "Conservative Slam at the Navy Seen as an Obstacle." I believe this is the same gentleman who wrote a book attacking the present Minister of Munitions and Supply and almost every other member of the cabinet, notwithstanding the fact that there is a war on. I was surprised to find this book in the library, in view of the statements it contains about members of the cabinet and of parliament. I have no quarrel whatever with the newspapers; as I said during the transportation fight in 1920 and 1921, you can never answer a newspaper because it always has the last word.
I did not raise this question on a motion to go into supply because that would prevent the minister from going on with his work, and personally I should like to see the house close by the end of the month, but I am only a private member. Any time I have spoken it has been at the request of the whip, though in addition I have asked a few questions. Of the matters I have brought up in the house, ninety-five per cent have been in an endeavour to secure better care, comfort and treatment for the members of his majesty's forces in this country. This article to which I have referred is grossly libelous, false, and malicious, and not for the public benefit. I have never criticized his majesty's forces at any time. Why should I criticize them? I have been working with them all my life, and I have a great number of friends in the army, navy and air force in both wars. As chairman of the Toronto harbour board I was a friend of the masters and mates' association on the great lakes when the working people on those boats and the merchant marine had far fewer friends than they have to-day. I object to this sort of scurrilous criticism, which is not criticism at all. This reporter gives a garbled account and no report at all of what happened in this chamber. Fair reports of the proceedings here are privileged, and rightly so; they may criti-size members of parliament as they wish, but cannot libel them. This was an unprovoked attack on me. I complain that the report of what I said was garbled, that this is not a fair report and no report at all, and that it has
War Appropriation-Supplies

caused me a great deal of damage in that it has advertised me as public enemy No. 1 of the men who are serving with such courage on land, on sea and, in the air, when I have served so faithfully our forces all these years.
Then in the Montreal Star of last Thursday the same columnist added insult to injury, when he said that the house witnessed the resumption of an exchange between myself and one of the ministers, and again accused me of attacking the navy. I said, "How could I attack the Canadian navy when in 1926 to 1928 there was no navy to attack?" I was referring to the peace-time strength of the navy, in 1926, and I was not the only one to criticize it. This very newspaper was one of the chief critics of the policy of the government of that day which was throwing away our defences, especially the navy to which we owe so much. I am not going to fire off a rifle to attack a mosquito, but I am not going to put up with this sort of thing any longer. I am a Conservative; I have never been anything else, but I was a progressive Conservative long before that name was adopted by my party. I told my leader why I could not go to Winnipeg, and he was satisfied with my reason. Since the beginning of the war we have had an honourable agreement among the parties of this house that the war is to be paramount and that politics should be put on the khelf for the duration. That is what I have been faithfully doing. I have not thought about being a Conservative; the issue is too sacred and grave for that, with our men overseas rewriting such a glorious history of courage. The matter is too serious for us to be fighting among ourselves like cats and dogs for pure party advantage. That is about all 1 have to say in this connection. Mr. Harold Ickes, one of the members of Mr. Roosevelt's administration has called columnists like this gentleman calumnists, and that is exactly what he is. He has double-crossed both parties; he is crosseyed; he has double-crossed* almost every minister on the front benches to-day; he has attacked the Prime Minister, the three ministers of defence, the Minister of Munitions and Supply, and others. I do not care anything about him, and I am sorry I have paid so much attention to him.
There are one or two matters I wish to bring before the committee, though not in any critical spirit because, as you know, since the war started I have given independent support to the government as long as we had a total war effort ; but what is meant by a total war effort' is something else again. I have been a consistent supporter of free enterprise in this country. The stand taken this afternoon by the leader of the opposition is all right. He I Mr. Church.]
stated that the Aluminum company is part of an international cartel, and that the government seems more or less helpless to do anything about world combinations of this kind. Then he went on to say that some international commission should be set up to deal with cartels and combines, so that the worker, the farmer and the small business man could be protected, and international rates and regulations established. That is all right as far as it goes; I have no objection to that policy, but I can say that I do not believe in all this international business. What was it Mr. Benes said here the other day: "I want to return to my own country." When the war is over there still will be independent nations, because patriotism is the cement that holds nations together. The people of the countries of Europe that have been overrun by the axis will want to return and rebuild their owm countries. There will always be nations; there will always be international trade, and I do not believe there is much use in sending a lot of college professors to Washington to talk about international debts, international exchange and so on. There will always be nations as long as time lasts.
I have referred to these matters on previous occasions. I was one of the pioneers in the hydro-electric development of Ontario, with many of our late leaders in this province, Sir James Whitney and Sir Adam Beck. We were blackguarded up and down the province; we were called amateur anarchists by one of the newspapers, but we took all the private franchises out of the counties of York, Ontario and Peel, and eventually all over the province. This was a people's movement for cheap light and power for all the people, and the leaders were not all of one party. I know of three or four hon. gentlemen across the chamber who were heads of municipalities and who took a great deal of interest then in this movement. This war is altogether different from the last one. I have a great deal of sympathy with hon. members to my left in what they say in some respects about public ownership of light, power and transportation. But we have to consider Quebec's own constitution, and the decision of the privy council. The province gave -its water power to private enterprise, and a few yeans ago what is known in the Saguenay river as the Shipshaw deal, and spent $35,000,000 in developing it. Already in a great many ways the government has taken the responsibility for this aluminum transaction as a war measure.
As I said on February 25, 1943, when speaking about private enterprise, I believe the first thing to do after the war is to encourage private initiative and free enterprise. True it

War Appropriation-Supplies
is, that this will have to be brought up to date. I believe that when the soldiers come home they will want the rights that men enjoyed in the days of Macdonald and Laurier, when everybody owned some property. It might be a cow; it might be a small mill or a country store, or a horse and waggon, but it was property of some kind. We have been slow to see that, with the right of acquiring private property denied to them, the people of Canada became proletarian. Their liberty passed away; it will have to be restored. I believe in private initiative. I believe that the right to possess private property is derived from nature and not from man, and that the state has no business to abolish it, but can only regulate its use.
Those are my views, and they are honest views. I believe that would be the view of the soldiers when they come home. In my opinion you can have all the planning you like, but neither victory nor any kind of planning will ever bring about the millennium. In a debate last January in the British House of Commons, Admiral Southby quoted the language of Strube, who has immortalized "The Little Man" who saved England in this war. He goes on to refer to the little man who saved England, saved them in the raids over London, and at Dieppe and at Dunkirk. "The little man" personifies the spirit of the mother country, the spirit of free enterprise and freedom of both retailers and wholesalers. The said little man who is the embodiment of British common sense and sanity to beat Hitler and Mussolini will be quite at home to defeat bureaucracy.
We have been slow in this House of Commons in not sooner opposing giving up our control over water power for war-time purposes. I do not blame the minister altogether for this particular stand he has taken. I have known him as long as anyone has known him. I knew him when he was a civil engineer. I have had a great deal of respect for him, because I know he was an expert in his business. When he came to this house he was not a politician.
We on this side of the house have forgotten that we have been politicians. The opposition has given the government splendid, independent war support, if for a total war. I am only one of the humble members of the opposition, but I have been here for a long time now and I have yet to change my views on this question. I believe that "the little man" who saved England, as Strube has said:
We who in the ashes dwell
Want no planned and ordered hell;
Fight no war to be policed
When the bombs and fires have ceased.
Life's too precious far to give
For any freedom but to live.
The mother country was built up on free enterprise. That is what made this empire. We came into being by the sea, and we cannot exist without the sea. Our first duty is to the mother country. I do not know about international agreements, because we were told by Mr. Churchill that we had made certain international agreements, and that Canada was a party to them. So was New Zealand, so was Australia, and so were other dominions. I do not know whether the government can tell us what those international agreements are, or what international settlements are to come.
I believe in the public ownership of the water powers of this country. It should be owned by the people, and developed for the benefit of the people in all the provinces joined together at confederation. When I first entered the house I asked for a national hydroelectric policy. We have in this country
42,000.000 horse-power in the aggregate. Of that amount only about 7,000,000 horse-power has been developed, part of it only seasonal. That water power belongs to the people. That is what the late Theodore Roosevelt believed in, and what the present President of the United States believed in, when he was governor of the state of New York.
The first duty of the yes-men in Germany is to find out what the fuehrer wants and then to make the planets dance to his desires. Yes-men are not all astrologers; it is a pity they are not. They would be better for it. They exist in all classes of society and in all communities, and their mark everywhere is the dread of freedom. These authoritarian governments-Germany, Italy and Japan-exist only by reason of yes-men and nodders. When a leader emerges he is acclaimed by them and he drives the country to ruin to their resounding cheers. No opposition is possible in the dictator-ridden countries. That is true, but the evolution of tyranny in Germany, Italy and Japan is possible only because of those who were ready to surrender to usurpation, and one fuehrer, duce, or what-not dictator. Saddled, they cannot be unseated without a general upset and by force and revolution. In Canada we can speak our minds.
There are one or two observations I should like to make about this particular deal. There has been no Gallup poll in connection with it. This Gallup poll is one of the most mischievous institutions this country ever had. We have evidence of it every day in the week. We did not have this Gallup poll in the days of our fight for cheap light and power in Ontario. This was copied from A1 Smith of New York, who twenty years ago called a straw vote. Where is the censorship to-day, especially with the parliamentary association
meeting here in Canada? Where is the censor
War Appropriation-Supplies

to-day, when this Gallup poll is on and we are allowing all this talk about forty-nine per cent being for the mother country and twenty-one per cent in favour of joining the United States. I say that is wrong. We didi not have that poll in the days to which I refer.
While I do not altogether like this particular transaction, and a lot of things done in the name of war, I do not like surrendering any further power to our beloved' allies of Russia and the United States. They say that we should forget all about the empire, and that we do not owe anything to the empire. In answer to that, I say that we are allied to two very powerful friends, two very powerful allies-Russia and the United States. They may not be imperial in the sense that they want more territory. That remains to be seen. But they are imperial in the sense that they want a larger share in the peace and as world powers and a better state of affairs when this war is over. And when it is over they will have something to say about the peace terms, and without our empire we will be lost.
I hope the minister will have due regard to this fact, that the surrender of our military and political initiative and of our resources to our friends in the United States is one of the vital mistakes we have made in this war, and brought about by the absolutely criminal defenceless position of this country when war came, because that is what it was. Not one party alone is to blame. All parties almost aided disarmament. We threw away our defences and our friends, with the result that when war broke out we had to start all over again. Let us remember that the United States need Great Britain the same as Great Britain needs the United States. It is not Great Britain's fight alone; it is America's fight as well. We are allies and friends. The people of the United States need us as much as we need them. We are allies, and we must see this thing through together.
I have 'been much displeased with some of what I have read of t'he record of the proceedings at Washington. These are the words of Lord Haig in the most critical days of the war of 1918, which is our motto now.
The safety of our homes and the freedom of mankind depend on each one of us at this critical moment being of good cheer. The British empire will win in the end. People's thoughts on war should not be distracted by secondary matters to a total war.
I was going to ask the Minister of Munitions and Supply one or two matters about this particular transaction on the Saguenay river, and about the settlement of war contracts after the war. This is a very large country. One of the vital mistakes we made

was that at the close of the last war hundreds of thousands of men and women who had been working in war work, and men who had been overseas were out of jobs. We should not make the same mistake this time.
This matter has been referred to in Washington, in an article in the March, 1943, issue of the National City Bank Review. It speaks of the dislocation of business and of working capital, and the cost of unemployment. Let us not forget the millions of workers in the munitions plants. In addition to them, there are those who are at war and who will come home. It goes on:
For there is involved the question whether the industries will be able to take up peacetime work quickly after their war work is over, or whether their working capital will be frozen in war production and its release subject to interminable delays and litigation.
This concerns a great many people. It concerns the possibly twenty million persons who will be working in the war industries, most of whom will need peace time jobs after war production is suspended. It concerns the millions in the armed forces who will be back looking for work after peace is restored. It concerns all who sell to the industries now producing war products, and all who will be looking for a market among their workers.
The producers of automobiles, radios, farm machinery and consumers' durable goods generally, who have converted wholly or in large part to production of a different kind than they normally carry on, will be particularly affected.
Reference is made to the dislocation of business that will occur, especially in Canada where production to-day is ten times what it was in the last war. It is also suggested that there should be a standard form of contract regarding payment. It continues:
Promulgation of such a code during the rvar w-ould prevent confusion and avert friction after the war. Necessarily the code would be on general lines, for except as to the elements of cost there can be no one method of keeping books which can fit the character and provisions of all contracts or be equally acceptable to everyone concerned. Nevertheless, it would seem practicable to set forth principles which would make it feasible for the government to approve the method of bookkeeping that a contractor is following, or to tell him what method he should follow on a specific contract.
The hope is expressed that we shall not have a repetition of what happenedi after the last war, when it took years and years to settle up. It is proposed that there should be an immediate part payment made on account. I commend these suggestions to the minister. I am a public ownership man and I have never faltered in that belief. I do not know everything about this deal, but I think it is a bad one. I am sorry the people of Quebec did not long ago adopt the principles which I thought they would, of taking over the water powers of the province for the benefit of the people. I would refer hon. members to what happened

War Appropriation-Supplies
years ago in connection with the Beauhamois deal and the proposed give-away of all the water powers in the Ottawa valley in 1927, which I opposed. This happened, and the opposition opposed it and won in 1927, and it went on for many weeks.
I have a great deal of sympathy with what in some ways hon. gentlemen to the left say. I have always been a supporter of public ownership. The government of the dhy will have to take the responsibility for this contract as a war measure to defeat Hitler. The minister probably cannot give us all the information we should like to have about it and about the international agreements which have been made, no doubt, with our allies regarding this work, but we can all rejoice in the fact that although in Munitions and Supply we made a slow start, the work which has been done since the war got under way is commendable and is a splendid chapter on the whole. No doubt mistakes have been made. I remember about three years before the war, in 1937, I suggested that a national registry should be madte of all wholesale and retail plants in the country to find out what each one could do. I was sure that war was coming. I suggested in 1938 that food reservoirs be set up in the old country and that there should be a survey of labour, a survey of water power, a survey of all large and small industrial plants and a survey of shipbuilding plants.
I hope before the minister finishes that he will have something to say about this fifty-mile limitation on bus travel by soldiers. The minister comes from a soldiering family and I do hope he will be able to make some change in this rule. When we took over the street railways in Toronto we had a clause inserted in the act which gave the city power to go into the operation of buses. This has proved a great help to the counities surrounding Toronto as well as the rest of Ontario. The people would not be able to get to the munitions plants if it were not for these buses. There should be some change in this rule, especially for the buses operating out of Oamp Borden. Last Sunday we had a bad storm and many of these soldiers were dumped off at a town eleven miles from Barrie and had to walk in.
Some consideration should be given to the need for the extension of certain health and essential public utilities, such as sewers, water supply and that kind of thing; the necessary steel should be released. Something should also be done in connection with housing. I have seen some of the effects of bad housing in the city of Toronto, and I appeal to the minister to do something to relieve the people of the great burden they are carrying.
In conclusion, may I repeat a quotation from Lord Perry I gave before, as follows:
The industrial revolution made it possible for any man to work his own way from poverty and illiteracy to a commanding position in both industry and the state. Richard Cobden is an outstanding example-the son of a Sussex farm labourer who became a great Lancashire manufacturer and a great statesman. William Cobbett is another example. In fact, industry and commerce during the nineteenth century produced such men not by the hundreds but by the thousands-careful, frugal men, hard of head and often hard of heart, but notable for two qualities above all others, diligence and self-reliance.
These men were self trained into habits of clear commercial thinking, quick and bold decisions, personal responsibility and individual initiative. It was no easy school. Those who lacked the necessary application or the necessary drive had short shrift. The age was kindly only to those who satisfied its needs.
We do not want a repetition of what happened after the Napoleonic and other wars, as outlined in the "History of England," by T. H. Green, Lord Shaftsbury and other historians. We do not want similar conditions to occur in our cities and towns and on our farms. I commend the hon. gentlemen to my left for the part they have taken in this movement. It follows the many reforms which have been brought about in Ontario by the Conservatives with regard to cheap power. I have referred to some of these to-day and there are others. I have grave doubt whether the state has been adequately protected in this Shipshaw deal, but it has been recommended by the minister and by the government, and they will have to take the responsibility. No doubt some of the terms are improvident.
I had a similar experience in connection with the Chippawa deal in the last war when that great plant was a blessing to Canada. It was said at one time in the last war that Ontario was supplying one-half the munitions for the mother country and the allies, and this was possible only because we had cheap power. The water powers of this country should belong to the people. I have great sympathy with the minister who has recommended this particular transaction. I realize that when the deal was consummated there was a grave situation existing. It was predicted after the fall of France that the British empire was done.
I have spoken to-night because I have been attacked. Never on any occasion have I been anything but a friend of the men and women, and the dependents of the men and women who are serving in this war. Yet this attack has been made in this newspaper, and I am being advertised all over Canada as enemy No. 1 of the men in the services. I have

War Appropriation-Supplies

always fought their battles since I have been a member. I want hon. members to know that I have found this house to be a place of much kindness. I have known most of the members for many years and I know they have done splendid work. Some of the best men we have came up here through the municipalities, and when brickbats are thrown at members of parliament it is simply an effort to prevent us from doing our duties as members.

I believe it will be in order under this item to discuss the question of the moneys expended by the government or by the minister and his department in connection with the making of industrial alcohol. I know the minister has promised to make a statement on this question, but I should like to say a little about it and to ask a few questions before that statement is made.
Without doubt the people of western Canada are greatly concerned, and rightly so, about this matter, because they consider that not only have we during this present war emergency conducted our affairs in a way which has not been to our greatest advantage, but that in the spending of moneys for the production of industrial alcohol the future of western Canada has been neglected. From various bodies in western Canada resolutions have been coming in possibly to other western members as well as myself showing the amount of interest which the people of the west are displaying in this question. It is said by certain people that the making of industrial alcohol and synthetic rubber from our large surplus stocks of wheat is a much better way of producing synthetic rubber than from petroleum. I think, when the minister makes his statement, it should be a very full and comprehensive one. I think he should place before the committee the detailed figures that were submitted to him, and let us know from what sources these figures were obtained so that we might be satisfied as to the correctness of the decisions made in this matter. Of course the minister will readily understand that there are very few members of the house who are competent to speak on these technical matters. I certainly am not, and therefore in matters of this kind we are obliged to go to sources which we believe are informed.
Like many other western people, I have been reading a pamphlet recently written by one of our young Canadian scientists, a man from the city of Winnipeg, Mr. Dyson Carter, M.Sc., A.C.I.C., F.C.G.S., registered professional engineer and research consulting science correspondent. The pamphlet he has called, "So that Man may Prosper", and in

this pamphlet he gives many facts and figures in substantiation of the claim that it would have been a better thing for Canada both in the war emergency and for the future if we had built distilleries and used our surplus stocks of wheat for the production of industrial alcohol and synthetic rubber. He makes the statement:
To produce from petroleum the butadiene required to make 200,000 tons of Buna rubber per year requires equipment costing $650,000,000.
But, he says:
To get butadiene from wheat is quite a different chemical problem, a far simpler one, requiring far less complicated equipment. This is summed up in the fact that to produce from wheat the butadiene required to make 200,000 tons of Buna rubber per year requires equipment costing only $30,000,000.
He also states that to assemble and build the plants, first of all the distilleries for processing the grain, would take roughly only about eight months, but that to build a plant and assemble machinery for the process which uses petroleum as a base takes at least eighteen months or a little longer. Therefore, from the point of view of the war emergency, his argument is that it would have been advisable for us to have built distilleries to use grain.
It is, I believe, a significant fact also that one of the united nations which has made a marvellous contribution in this war, a nation which has unlimited quantities of petroleum and could have used that as a base, if it were advantageous to do so, has nevertheless thought it necessary and expedient to use large quantities of grain for making industrial alcohol. That country, of course, is the Soviet Union. It is, I believe, a well-known fact that engineers and research men from the Soviet Union offered their services at one time to the United States government and offered to give all the information and help necessary to enable the United States to proceed with this process themselves. But the United States had as its advisers some dollar-a-year men who were connected with the great oil corporations and these men prevented the Russian research men from coming to the United States and giving their assistance.
It would be a good thing, I think, if the minister would give some indication whether we in this country were offered any help by any other country on this question and whether we appealed to any other country for suggestions and help when we knew that this process was being used elsewhere.
It is perhaps something which the general public does not know very well, but it should know, that these giant oil corporations in the United States which have subsidiaries in this country, Standard Oil particularly, were guilty

The same oil corporations which sold the secrets to Germany and Italy refused to sell the same secrets to their own United States government until that government forced them to do so.

alcohol. Instead of malt they use a special "mold," similar to the kind of mold that makes bread spoil. Details of the mold and the method of using it cannot be released at this time, because the process is of vital military importance to the united nations.

The Seagram Company (known in Canada mostly for the liquor it manufactures, but familiar to chemists as one of the world's largest producers of industrial alcohol) has announced that its famous Russian-American scientist, Dr. Paul J. Kolachov, has perfected a revolutionary new system of fermenting mash. The new process is continuous. Instead of fermenting the mash in enormous batches, the Kolachov apparatus carries out the process continuously. . . .
Chemical engineers are well acquainted with this method applied to industrial processes. Thus in the continuous fermentation process for making alcohol, the time required for complete fermentation is reduced from 50 hours to only 5 hours. In effect this makes one piece of apparatus do the work of ten. The cost of erecting large-scale equipment is thus drastically reduced, and the cost of production of alcohol considerably lowered. The new method is therefore expected to have a very favourable effect upon the future manufacture of industrial alcohol from wheat. . . .
When wheat is fermented to make alcohol, naturally a large quantity of fermented mash is left behind. Most of the starch in the wheat has been removed from this material, in the form of alcohol. The remaining mash is thus rich in wheat proteins. And1 proteins are the food substances that build muscle-meat-in cattle and chickens. . . .
When large-scale grain alcohol plants are established in the farm lands, the farmers will have a source of feed of the highest quality. This feed will be a by-product of the alcohol industry. In this way the cost of raising beef cattle, sheep, hogs and poultry will be sharply reduced. There will be a large and dependable source of supply of the feed. And the feed will be one of the finest known to science. This combination of advantages will place the wheat farmer in a very much better position for carrying on mixed farming, a matter of vital concern in post-war Canada.
When our people in western Canada read of these things, they realize that vast horizons would open out to them if only they were in the position to establish the basis, which is the industrial alcohol, for many of the new industrial uses to which it could be put. Will this war not determine whether we are to go on, in the future, as we have too largely in the past, ever seeking to emphasize the differences between nations and between individuals, or whether "men's lives are to be levelled up as well as levelled down-levelled up in their common inner meaning, levelled down in their outer gloriousness and show!"
Hear, hear.

"Hear, hear" yes, but fine words butter no parsnips. Here are these workers in Quebec who work side by side with other employees in the same plaint under poorer conditions, and I say that we should keep in mind that these men, even if they are workers, are still men, with all the hopes and aspirations of human beings. Let me say in conclusion that we cannot educate men and women and put the light of life in their souls, and then treat them as mere serfs or as bits of material no better than the raw materials that enter into production.

The other day when the estimates of the Minister of National Defence were up for discussion I asked a few questions which were not completely answered, and perhaps the Minister of Munitions and Supply can cover the ground a little more thoroughly. I was asking questions with respect to the salvaging of materials after the work on a plant or building had been completed. My understanding is that contracts for the erection of buildings are made out and signed, and that there is no salvaging so far as the government is concerned of any materials that may be left over, that any left-over materials are sold perhaps by the contractor, who may get whatever he can out of them, and that the country gets no benefit from the sale. If that be so, I would ask the minister what check is made of materials going into new buildings and what check is made of the materials that may be left over when a job is completed. I know for a fact that in the building of a certain air training school vast quantities of materials were left over, mostly lumber, and they were not salvaged so far as any government salvaging is concerned.

May I ask my hon. friend a question? I think he asked for a return on that matter, and if I remember the contract, it was a lump sum contract, and the materials belonged to the contractor. Is that the contract?
